questions.question: What is an exception in Java?
questions.answer:
An event that disrupts the normal flow of a program, such as dividing by zero, reading a missing file or calling a method on null. It's handled with try / catch / finally.

  • Checked (e.g. IOException, SQLException): checked at compile time, so you must catch them or declare them with throws.
  • Unchecked (subclasses of RuntimeException, e.g. NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException): usually programming errors, and they don't need declaring.
  • Error (e.g. OutOfMemoryError): serious JVM problems the app usually shouldn't handle.

questions.question: What's the difference between throw and throws?
questions.answer:
throw actually throws an exception. throws declares in a method signature that the method might throw one.

public void read(String p) throws IOException {
  if (p == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("null path");
}

questions.question: What is try-with-resources?
questions.answer:
A try block (Java 7+) that automatically closes resources implementing AutoCloseable, like files, streams and database connections, even if an exception happens.

try (var r = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("a.txt"))) {
  r.readLine();
}

questions.question: What are good practices for exception handling?
questions.answer:
• Catch specific exceptions, not a broad Exception.
  • Never swallow exceptions with an empty catch block. At least log them.
  • Use finally or try-with-resources for cleanup.
  • Create custom exceptions for business errors, e.g. InvalidQuoteException.
  • Don't use exceptions for normal control flow.

questions.question: Does Java have structs?
questions.answer:
No. You group data with a class or, since Java 16, a record. A record's fields are final (shallowly immutable), and it generates the constructor, accessor methods, equals, hashCode and toString, so it's the closest thing to a struct.

public record Policy(String id, double premium) {}
policy.premium(); // accessors are named after the field, not getPremium()

questions.question: What are the main Java collections?
questions.answer:
• List (ArrayList, LinkedList): ordered, allows duplicates.
  • Set (HashSet, TreeSet): no duplicates.
  • Map (HashMap, TreeMap): key–value pairs.
  • Queue / Deque (ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue): FIFO, stack or priority ordering.

questions.question: What are Java's primitive types?
questions.answer: Eight: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean. Everything else, including String, arrays and collections, is an object (reference type). Each primitive has a wrapper class, like Integer for int.

questions.question: What's the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
questions.answer: == compares references (whether it's the same object in memory), or values for primitives. .equals() compares content. Always use .equals() for Strings: "a".equals(s).

questions.question: What's the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
questions.answer:
• Abstract class: can have state (fields), constructors and both implemented and abstract methods. A class can extend only one.
  • Interface: a contract of methods, which can include default methods but no instance state. A class can implement many.

Use an interface for "can do" capabilities and an abstract class for shared base behaviour.

questions.question: What does final mean in Java?
questions.answer:
• final variable: can't be reassigned.
  • final method: can't be overridden.
  • final class: can't be extended (e.g. String).

questions.question: What's the difference between Kotlin and Java?
questions.answer:
Both run on the JVM and interoperate, so a project can mix the two and share libraries. Kotlin is more modern and concise:

  • Null safety in the type system (String vs String?), so many null bugs are caught at compile time.
  • Data classes remove boilerplate.
  • Type inference with val / var, and no semicolons.
  • Coroutines for simpler async code.
  • No checked exceptions.

questions.question: What's the difference between val and var in Kotlin?
questions.answer: val is read-only: it can't be reassigned, like Java's final. var is mutable. Prefer val by default.

questions.question: How does null safety work in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
Types are non-null by default. Add ? to allow null. Then use:

  • ?. safe call: name?.length
  • ?: Elvis operator: name ?: "Unknown"
  • ?.let { } to run code only when the value isn't null
  • !! asserts non-null (throws if null, so avoid it)

Values coming from Java code have "platform types", so Kotlin can't check them: treat them as nullable.

questions.question: What is a data class in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
A class for holding data that auto-generates equals, hashCode, toString, copy and destructuring.

data class User(val name: String, val age: Int)

questions.question: What is Quarkus?
questions.answer: A Java/Kotlin framework for building cloud-native microservices. It's known for fast startup and low memory use, works well in containers and Kubernetes, and supports REST APIs, dependency injection and Kafka. It's similar in purpose to Spring Boot.

questions.question: What are coroutines in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
A lightweight way to write asynchronous code that reads like normal code. A suspend function can pause, for example while waiting for a network call, without blocking the thread.

  • launch starts a coroutine and doesn't return a result.
  • async returns a Deferred, and you get its result with await().
  • Dispatchers.IO is for blocking I/O work, and Dispatchers.Default for CPU-heavy work.

Coroutines run inside a scope. When the scope is cancelled, its coroutines are cancelled too. This is called structured concurrency.

questions.question: What are extension functions in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
They add a method to an existing class without changing it or subclassing it.

fun String.isEmail(): Boolean = contains("@")

"a@b.com".isEmail()  // true

They are resolved at compile time, so they can't override a real member, and they can't access private members.

questions.question: What is a sealed class in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
A class whose subclasses are all known at compile time, because they must be declared in the same package and module. This lets when check that every case is covered, with no else needed:

sealed interface Result
data class Success(val data: String) : Result
data class Error(val message: String) : Result

when (result) {
    is Success -> show(result.data)
    is Error -> showError(result.message)
}

If you add a new subclass later, the compiler shows you every when you need to update.

questions.question: What are scope functions in Kotlin (let, run, with, apply, also)?
questions.answer:
They run a block of code on an object. They differ in how you refer to the object and in what they return:

  • let: object is it, returns the block's result. Often used with ?.let for null checks.
  • run: object is this, returns the block's result.
  • with(obj): like run, but you pass the object in as an argument.
  • apply: object is this, returns the object. Good for setting it up.
  • also: object is it, returns the object. Good for side effects like logging.

questions.question: What's the difference between lateinit and by lazy?
questions.answer:
• lateinit var: a non-null var you promise to set before using it, e.g. in a setup method or by dependency injection. Reading it before then throws an exception. It can't be used with primitive types like Int.
  • val x by lazy { ... }: a read-only value worked out the first time it's used and then cached. It's thread-safe by default.

questions.question: What are object and companion object in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
• object declares a singleton: a class with exactly one instance, created when first used.
  • companion object sits inside a class and holds members you call on the class itself, like User.create(). Kotlin has no static keyword, so this fills that role. Add @JvmStatic if Java code should see a real static method.

questions.question: What's the difference between JavaScript and TypeScript?
questions.answer: TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript that adds static typing. JS checks types only at runtime. TS catches type errors at compile time, in the editor. TS adds interfaces, generics and enums, gives better autocomplete and refactoring, and compiles to plain JS. It's especially valuable on large codebases and teams.

questions.question: What's any vs unknown in TypeScript?
questions.answer: any turns off type checking, so avoid it. unknown means "type not known yet", and TS forces you to check it (e.g. typeof x === "string") before using it. That makes it the safer choice.

questions.question: What's the difference between interface and type in TypeScript?
questions.answer: Both describe object shapes. Interfaces can be extended and merged. type is more flexible: it can express unions ('draft' | 'bound'), primitives and tuples. In practice they're often interchangeable.

questions.question: Do TypeScript types exist at runtime?
questions.answer: No. They're erased when TS compiles to JS. So data from APIs or user input still needs runtime validation (e.g. with Zod or manual checks).

questions.question: What's the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
questions.answer: == compares after type coercion, so '5' == 5 is true. === compares value and type, so '5' === 5 is false. Use ===.

questions.question: What's the difference between let, const and var?
questions.answer:
• var: function-scoped, hoisted and initialised to undefined. Avoid it.
  • let: block-scoped, can be reassigned.
  • const: block-scoped, can't be reassigned. An object or array it holds can still be changed.

let and const are hoisted too, but using them before the declaration throws (the "temporal dead zone"). Default to const, and use let when the value must change.

questions.question: What is a Promise, and what does async/await do?
questions.answer:
A Promise represents a value that will be available later: pending, then fulfilled or rejected. async/await is a cleaner syntax for working with Promises, so async code reads like sync code. Use try/catch for errors.

async function load() {
  const res = await fetch("/api/quotes");
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

A common trap: fetch only rejects on network failure. A 404 or 500 still resolves, so check res.ok.

questions.question: What is Vue.js, and what does v-model do?
questions.answer: Vue is a progressive JavaScript framework for building UIs from reusable components with reactive data. v-model creates two-way binding between a form input and component state, so typing updates the data and changing the data updates the input.

questions.question: How do you create a form in HTML?
questions.answer:
Use <form> with an action (where data goes) and a method (usually POST). Inside it, add <input>, <select>, <textarea> and a submit button.

  • Each field needs a name or its value isn't sent.
  • Link <label for> to the input's id for accessibility.
  • Built-in validation: required, type="email", min, pattern.
  • In apps, handle submit in JS with preventDefault() and fetch.

questions.question: What's the difference between GET and POST?
questions.answer:
GET retrieves data. Parameters go in the URL, so it can be cached, bookmarked and shared; it should have no side effects, and you should never put passwords or tokens in it, because URLs end up in logs and history. POST sends data in the request body to create or submit something, like a form.

GET (like PUT and DELETE) is idempotent: repeating it has the same effect. POST isn't, which is why browsers warn before resubmitting a form.

questions.question: What is a REST API?
questions.answer:
An API built around resources (nouns in the URL, like /quotes/42) and HTTP methods:

  • GET: read
  • POST: create
  • PUT: replace the whole resource; PATCH: change part of it
  • DELETE: remove

It's stateless (each request carries everything the server needs, such as the auth token), usually returns JSON, and uses status codes to report the result: 201 after a create, 404 for a missing resource.

questions.question: What do common HTTP status codes mean?
questions.answer:
• 2xx success: 200 OK · 201 Created · 204 No Content
  • 3xx redirect: 301 Moved Permanently · 302 Found (temporary) · 304 Not Modified (use your cached copy)
  • 4xx client error: 400 Bad Request · 401 Unauthorized (not logged in) · 403 Forbidden (no permission) · 404 Not Found · 409 Conflict · 422 Unprocessable (valid JSON, invalid data) · 429 Too Many Requests
  • 5xx server error: 500 Internal Server Error · 502 Bad Gateway · 503 Service Unavailable

questions.question: What are some secure coding practices for web apps?
questions.answer:
• Validate and sanitise all input on the server. Never trust the client.
  • Use parameterised queries to prevent SQL injection.
  • Escape output to prevent XSS, and add a Content Security Policy.
  • Protect forms that use cookie sessions against CSRF (SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens).
  • Use HTTPS, and hash passwords with a slow algorithm (argon2 or bcrypt).
  • Rate-limit login and other sensitive endpoints.
  • Least privilege, and keep secrets out of code.
  • Keep dependencies updated.

questions.question: What's the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?
questions.answer: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key is a column referencing another table's primary key, which links the tables, e.g. policies.customer_id → customers.id.

questions.question: What's the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
questions.answer:
INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, plus matches from the right, with NULL where there's no match.

SELECT c.name, p.id FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN policies p ON p.customer_id = c.id;

questions.question: What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, so it can use aggregates like COUNT(*) > 5.

questions.question: What is an index, and what's the trade-off?
questions.answer: A data structure (usually a B-tree) that speeds up lookups on a column, like a book's index. The trade-off: more storage, and slower INSERT/UPDATE because the index has to be maintained too.

questions.question: What is a transaction (ACID)?
questions.answer:
A group of operations that succeed or fail together.

  • Atomicity: all or nothing
  • Consistency: rules stay valid
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere
  • Durability: committed data survives crashes

Example: binding a policy and recording a payment should be one transaction.

questions.question: What are the four principles of OOP?
questions.answer:
• Encapsulation: hide internal state behind methods.
  • Inheritance: reuse behaviour from a parent class.
  • Polymorphism: one interface, different implementations.
  • Abstraction: expose only what's needed and hide complexity.

questions.question: What is SOLID?
questions.answer:
• Single responsibility: one reason to change.
  • Open/closed: open for extension, closed for modification.
  • Liskov substitution: subclasses can replace their parents.
  • Interface segregation: small, focused interfaces.
  • Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete classes.

questions.question: What's the difference between overloading and overriding?
questions.answer: Overloading: same method name, different parameters, in the same class (resolved at compile time). Overriding: a subclass provides its own implementation of a parent method with the same signature (resolved at runtime).

questions.question: What is Docker?
questions.answer: A tool that packages an app and its dependencies into a container, so it runs the same way everywhere, from a laptop to production. An image is the blueprint (built from a Dockerfile). A container is a running instance of an image.

questions.question: What is Kubernetes?
questions.answer: A platform that orchestrates containers: it deploys, scales, restarts failed containers, load-balances and rolls out updates across a cluster of machines.

questions.question: What is CI/CD?
questions.answer:
Continuous Integration: every change is automatically built and tested when it's pushed, so problems surface within minutes.

Continuous Delivery: every change that passes is ready to release, and deploying to production is one click. Continuous Deployment goes one step further: changes that pass go to production automatically, with no manual step.

Either way releases are small and frequent, which makes them less risky and easier to roll back.

questions.question: What's the difference between git merge and git rebase?
questions.answer: Merge combines branches with a merge commit and keeps the history as it happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch for a linear history. Don't rebase shared branches others are working on.

questions.question: What are unit, integration and end-to-end tests?
questions.answer:
• Unit: tests one function or class in isolation. Fast, and the most numerous.
  • Integration: tests components working together, e.g. an API plus the database.
  • E2E: tests the whole app the way a user would, e.g. completing a quote in the browser.

questions.question: What is Agile / Scrum?
questions.answer: Agile is an iterative way of working: small increments, frequent feedback, adapting to change. Scrum is a framework for it, with sprints (usually 2 weeks), daily stand-ups, sprint planning, review and a retrospective. Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master and the dev team.

questions.question: What is Kafka?
questions.answer: A distributed event-streaming platform. Producers publish messages to topics, and consumers read them. Services can communicate asynchronously and reliably, e.g. a "policy bound" event triggering emails, invoicing and reporting.

questions.question: What are microservices?
questions.answer: An architecture where an app is split into small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and talking over APIs or events. Pros: independent scaling and deployment. Cons: more operational complexity, network calls and harder debugging.

questions.question: What is Big O notation?
questions.answer:
A way to describe how an algorithm's time or memory grows as the input grows. It's an upper bound, usually quoted for the worst case, and ignores constants.

  • O(1): constant, e.g. a hash map lookup (on average)
  • O(log n): binary search
  • O(n): looping through a list
  • O(n log n): efficient sorts (merge sort)
  • O(n²): nested loops

questions.question: What's the difference between an array and a linked list?
questions.answer:
• Array: contiguous memory, O(1) access by index, but inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n) because elements shift.
  • Linked list: nodes point to the next node, O(1) insert/delete once you're at the node, but O(n) access because you walk the list.

questions.question: What's the difference between a stack and a queue?
questions.answer: Stack: LIFO (last in, first out), like a pile of plates. Push and pop. Used for undo and the call stack. Queue: FIFO (first in, first out), like a line. Enqueue and dequeue. Used for job processing and BFS.

questions.question: How does a hash map work?
questions.answer:
It runs the key through a hash function to get a bucket index, then stores the key–value pair there. Lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average.

A collision happens when two keys land in the same bucket; it's handled with a list or tree in that bucket. When the map gets too full (past its load factor), it grows and rehashes every entry, which is why inserts are O(1) amortised. In Java, keys need correct equals() and hashCode(), and shouldn't change while they're in the map.

questions.question: What is recursion?
questions.answer:
A function that calls itself to solve smaller versions of the same problem. It needs a base case to stop, otherwise you get a stack overflow.

int factorial(int n) {
  if (n <= 1) return 1;      // base case
  return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

questions.question: How does binary search work?
questions.answer: On a sorted array, check the middle element. If the target is smaller, search the left half; if larger, the right half. Repeat. Time is O(log n).

questions.question: Name some common sorting algorithms and their complexity.
questions.answer:
• Bubble / insertion sort: O(n²), simple but slow (insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted data).
  • Merge sort: O(n log n), stable, uses extra memory.
  • Quick sort: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) worst case, sorts in place.

In practice you use the built-in sort: Java's List.sort and JavaScript's Array.prototype.sort are stable. A JavaScript trap: with no comparator it sorts as strings, so [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9]. Use arr.sort((a, b) => a - b), or toSorted to keep the original.

questions.question: How would you find duplicates in an array efficiently?
questions.answer:
Loop through once with a HashSet. If an element is already in the set, it's a duplicate. That's O(n) time and O(n) space, compared with O(n²) for nested loops.

const seen = new Set();
for (const x of arr) { if (seen.has(x)) return x; seen.add(x); }

questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
A function that remembers the variables from the scope where it was created, even after that outer function has finished running.

function counter() {
  let count = 0;
  return () => ++count;
}
const next = counter();
next(); // 1
next(); // 2

Used for private state, callbacks and factories.

questions.question: What is the event loop?
questions.answer:
JavaScript runs on a single thread. Async work (timers, fetch) is handed off, and its callbacks wait in a queue. The event loop pushes them onto the call stack when the stack is empty. Microtasks (Promises) run before macrotasks (setTimeout).

console.log(1);
setTimeout(() => console.log(2));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3));
console.log(4);
// 1, 4, 3, 2

questions.question: How does this work in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
this depends on how a function is called:

  • As a method (obj.fn()): this is obj.
  • As a plain function: undefined in strict mode (and in modules and classes), the global object otherwise.
  • With new: the newly created object.
  • Arrow functions don't have their own this; they use the surrounding scope's.
  • call, apply and bind set it explicitly.

A classic bug: passing obj.fn as a callback loses this. Use an arrow function or bind.

questions.question: What is hoisting?
questions.answer: JavaScript moves declarations to the top of their scope before running code. var is hoisted and set to undefined. Function declarations are fully hoisted. let and const are hoisted but can't be used before their declaration (the "temporal dead zone").

questions.question: What do map, filter and reduce do?
questions.answer:
• map: transforms each item, returning a new array of the same length.
  • filter: keeps items that pass a test.
  • reduce: combines all items into one value.
const total = quotes
  .filter(q => q.status === "bound")
  .map(q => q.premium)
  .reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0);

questions.question: What are spread and destructuring?
questions.answer:
// Destructuring: pull values out
const { name, age } = user;
const [first, second] = list;

// Spread: copy or merge
const copy = { ...user, age: 30 };
const all = [...a, ...b];

Spread makes a shallow copy: nested objects are still shared.

questions.question: What is the CSS box model?
questions.answer: Every element is a box made of content → padding → border → margin (from inside out). By default width sets only the content. With box-sizing: border-box, width includes padding and border, which is easier to work with.

questions.question: What's the difference between Flexbox and Grid?
questions.answer: Flexbox is one-dimensional: it lays items out in a row or a column, and is great for nav bars, aligning items and spacing. Grid is two-dimensional: rows and columns at once, great for page layouts and card grids. They're often used together.

questions.question: How do you make a page responsive?
questions.answer:
• Add the viewport meta tag.
  • Use relative units (%, rem, vw) and flexible layouts (Flexbox/Grid).
  • Use media queries: @media (max-width: 768px) { ... }
  • Design mobile-first, and make images flexible with max-width: 100%.

questions.question: What is CSS specificity?
questions.answer: The rule for which style wins when several apply. From strongest to weakest: inline styles → IDs → classes, attributes, pseudo-classes → elements. If specificity is equal, the later rule wins. !important overrides everything, so avoid it.

questions.question: What's the difference between state and props in React?
questions.answer: Props are passed into a component from its parent and are read-only. State is data a component owns and can change with useState. Changing state re-renders the component.

questions.question: What do useState and useEffect do?
questions.answer:
• useState: adds state to a function component, returning [value, setValue]. Setting state schedules a re-render.
  • useEffect: runs side effects (subscriptions, timers, syncing with something outside React) after render. The dependency array controls when it reruns, and the function you return cleans up.
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id); // cleanup
}, []); // [] = run once after mount

In development, StrictMode runs effects twice on mount to expose missing cleanup. For fetching data, most apps use a library (TanStack Query) or their framework's data loading rather than a bare effect.

questions.question: What is the virtual DOM?
questions.answer:
A lightweight description of the UI kept in memory. When state changes, React renders a new tree, compares it with the previous one (reconciliation, or diffing), and applies only the differences to the real DOM.

The point isn't that it beats hand-written DOM updates; it lets you write the UI declaratively (describe what it should look like) while React works out the minimal changes.

questions.question: Why do lists in React need a key?
questions.answer: Keys help React identify which items changed, were added or were removed, so it can update the list efficiently and keep each item's state correct. Use a stable unique ID, not the array index if the list can reorder.

questions.question: How does React compare with Vue?
questions.answer: Both are component-based with a virtual DOM and reactive updates. React uses JSX (HTML-like syntax in JavaScript) and is a library, so routing and state come from separate packages. Vue uses HTML-based templates, has v-model for two-way binding, and includes more out of the box. Coming from React, Vue is quick to pick up.

questions.question: What does static mean in Java?
questions.answer: A static field or method belongs to the class, not to individual objects. All instances share it, and you call it without creating an object: Math.max(a, b). Static methods can't use this or instance fields directly.

questions.question: What are generics in Java?
questions.answer:
They let classes and methods work with any type while staying type-safe at compile time. List<String> can only hold Strings, so there's no casting and no runtime ClassCastException.

public <T> T first(List<T> list) { return list.get(0); }

questions.question: What are Streams and lambdas in Java?
questions.answer:
Lambdas (Java 8) are short anonymous functions: x -> x * 2. Streams process collections in a functional style:

double total = quotes.stream()
  .filter(q -> q.isBound())
  .mapToDouble(Quote::getPremium)
  .sum();

questions.question: What's the difference between String and StringBuilder?
questions.answer: String is immutable: every change creates a new object, so concatenating in a loop is slow. StringBuilder is mutable and efficient for building strings step by step. (StringBuffer is the older, thread-safe version.)

questions.question: What is garbage collection in Java?
questions.answer: The JVM automatically frees memory used by objects that are no longer referenced, so you don't free memory manually like in C. You can still leak memory by keeping references you don't need, e.g. in a static collection that keeps growing.

questions.question: What's the difference between JDK, JRE and JVM?
questions.answer:
• JVM: runs Java bytecode. It's what makes Java "write once, run anywhere."
  • JRE: the JVM plus the standard libraries needed to run apps.
  • JDK: the JRE plus development tools like the compiler (javac).

Since Java 11 there's no separate JRE download from Oracle: you install a JDK, and can build a trimmed runtime for your app with jlink.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot?
questions.answer: A popular Java framework for building web apps and REST APIs quickly. It provides dependency injection, auto-configuration, an embedded server and easy database access (Spring Data JPA). Quarkus is a newer alternative focused on fast startup in containers.

questions.question: What is .NET?
questions.answer:
Microsoft's free, open-source, cross-platform platform for building web apps, APIs, desktop and cloud apps, mainly in C#. Modern .NET (5 and later) is the successor to .NET Core and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS; the old .NET Framework (4.8) is Windows-only and kept for legacy apps.

Code compiles to intermediate language and runs on the CLR (Common Language Runtime), similar to Java's JVM. Even-numbered releases are long-term support: .NET 10 (with C# 14) is the current LTS, supported until November 2028, and .NET 8 and .NET 9 reached end of support on 10 November 2026.

questions.question: How does C# compare with Java?
questions.answer:
Very similar: both are statically typed, object-oriented and garbage-collected, and run on a virtual machine, and both now have var, records, lambdas and pattern matching. Differences you'll notice:

  • C# has properties (get; set;), LINQ, async/await and events built into the language.
  • C# has user-defined value types (struct) and nullable reference types.
  • Java has checked exceptions; C# doesn't.

Moving between them is fairly easy.

questions.question: What is ASP.NET Core?
questions.answer:
The .NET framework for building web apps and REST APIs. It's fast, cross-platform, has dependency injection built in, uses a middleware pipeline for requests, and supports MVC controllers or minimal APIs.

app.MapGet("/quotes/{id}", (int id) => GetQuote(id));

questions.question: What is LINQ?
questions.answer:
Language Integrated Query: lets you query collections and databases with C# syntax, similar to Java Streams or JS filter/map.

var total = quotes
  .Where(q => q.Status == "Bound")
  .Sum(q => q.Premium);

questions.question: What is Entity Framework Core?
questions.answer: The main ORM for .NET. It maps C# classes to database tables, so you can query with LINQ instead of writing raw SQL. It supports migrations to update the database schema from code, and works with SQL Server, PostgreSQL and others.

questions.question: What's the difference between a class and a struct in C#?
questions.answer: A class is a reference type: variables point to the same object on the heap. A struct is a value type: it's copied when assigned or passed, and is good for small, simple data like a point or a money amount. Unlike Java, C# does have structs.

questions.question: How does async/await work in C#?
questions.answer:
A method marked async returns a Task (or Task<T>). await pauses the method until the task completes without blocking the thread, so the server can handle other requests meanwhile.

public async Task<Quote?> GetQuoteAsync(int id)
{
    return await _db.Quotes.FindAsync(id); // null if not found
}

Use async all the way down for I/O (database, HTTP, files); it doesn't make CPU-bound work faster.

questions.question: What is dependency injection in ASP.NET Core?
questions.answer:
Services are registered in a built-in container, and the framework passes them into constructors automatically, so classes don't create their own dependencies. That makes code easier to test and swap.

builder.Services.AddScoped<IQuoteService, QuoteService>();

Lifetimes: Transient (new every time), Scoped (one per request), Singleton (one for the whole app).

questions.question: What's the difference between cookies, sessions and JWT?
questions.answer:
• Cookie: small data the browser stores and sends with every request to that site.
  • Session: the server stores the user's data and gives the browser a session ID (usually in a cookie). State lives on the server, so logging out or banning a user takes effect immediately.
  • JWT: a signed token holding the user's claims. The server doesn't store it, it just verifies the signature, which suits APIs and microservices.

JWTs are signed, not encrypted, so anyone can read them, and they can't easily be revoked before they expire: keep them short-lived and pair them with a refresh token.

questions.question: What is CORS?
questions.answer:
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. By default browsers block a page's JavaScript from reading responses from a different origin (domain, port or protocol). The server opts in by sending headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

For requests that aren't "simple" (a JSON body, custom headers, PUT or DELETE), the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request to ask permission. CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server, so it doesn't protect an API from scripts or curl: you still need authentication.

questions.question: What's the difference between authentication and authorisation?
questions.answer: Authentication: who are you? (logging in). Authorisation: what are you allowed to do? (permissions and roles). The 401 status means not authenticated; 403 means authenticated but not allowed.

questions.question: What happens when you type a URL into a browser?
questions.answer:
1. DNS looks up the domain's IP address.
  2. The browser opens a TCP connection, plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS.
  3. It sends an HTTP request, and the server returns HTML.
  4. The browser parses the HTML, loads CSS, JS and images, builds the DOM and renders the page.

questions.question: What are SQL injection and XSS, and how do you prevent them?
questions.answer:
• SQL injection: user input gets run as part of an SQL query. Prevent it with parameterised queries or an ORM, never string concatenation.
  • XSS (cross-site scripting): an attacker's script runs in other users' browsers. Prevent it by escaping output (frameworks do this by default), avoiding innerHTML with user data, and using a Content Security Policy.

questions.question: What is normalisation?
questions.answer: Organising tables to reduce duplicate data and avoid update errors, e.g. storing customer details once in a customers table and referencing them by ID from policies, instead of repeating them in every row. Sometimes you denormalise on purpose for read performance.

questions.question: What's the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?
questions.answer: SQL (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL): tables with a fixed schema, relationships, joins and strong ACID transactions, which suits financial and insurance data. NoSQL (MongoDB, Redis, DynamoDB): flexible schemas (documents, key–value), easy horizontal scaling, good for large or fast-changing data.

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem?
questions.answer: Loading a list with 1 query, then running 1 extra query per item to load related data, so 100 policies means 101 queries. It's common with ORMs. Fix it with a JOIN or eager loading (e.g. JOIN FETCH in JPA, .Include() in EF Core).

questions.question: What is the Singleton pattern?
questions.answer: Ensures a class has only one instance and provides global access to it, e.g. a configuration object or a logger. Overusing it creates hidden global state that makes testing harder. Dependency injection containers can manage single instances more cleanly.

questions.question: What is the Factory pattern?
questions.answer: A method or class that creates objects for you, so the calling code doesn't need to know the exact class. Example: PolicyFactory.create("home") returns a HomePolicy, and "car" returns a CarPolicy.

questions.question: What is the Observer pattern?
questions.answer: One object (the subject) notifies many subscribers (observers) when something changes, without knowing who they are. Examples: DOM event listeners, reactive state in Vue and React, and event systems like Kafka at a larger scale.

questions.question: What is MVC?
questions.answer:
Model–View–Controller separates an app into three parts:

  • Model: data and business logic.
  • View: what the user sees.
  • Controller: handles requests, uses the model and picks a view.

Used in Spring MVC, ASP.NET MVC and many web frameworks.

questions.question: What is dependency injection?
questions.answer: Instead of a class creating its own dependencies (new EmailService()), they're passed in, usually through the constructor. This makes code loosely coupled and easy to test, because you can pass a mock. Spring, Quarkus and ASP.NET Core all have DI built in.

questions.question: What is the Strategy pattern?
questions.answer: You put each version of an algorithm in its own class behind a shared interface, and choose one at runtime. Example: a PricingStrategy interface with StandardPricing and DiscountPricing. The calling code just calls strategy.price(order). This replaces long if/else chains. Java's Comparator works this way.

questions.question: What is the Builder pattern?
questions.answer:
It builds an object step by step, which helps when there are many optional fields and a constructor would get messy.

HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create(url))
    .header("Accept", "application/json")
    .build();

Lombok's @Builder generates one for you. Kotlin and C# rarely need it, because named and default arguments do the same job.

questions.question: What is the Adapter pattern?
questions.answer: It wraps a class so it matches an interface your code already expects, like a travel plug adapter. Example: your app uses a PaymentGateway interface, so you write a StripeAdapter that implements it and calls the Stripe SDK inside. If you switch provider later, you only write a new adapter.

questions.question: What is the Decorator pattern?
questions.answer: It adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object that has the same interface. The caller can't tell the difference. Example: new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file)) in Java adds buffering on top of plain reading. You could also wrap a UserService in a CachingUserService to add caching without changing the original class.

questions.question: What is the Repository pattern?
questions.answer: It hides data access behind an interface with methods like findById, save and delete. Business logic calls the repository and never sees SQL or the database. This keeps code tidy and makes testing easy, because you can swap in a fake repository. Spring Data JPA generates repositories for you, and in .NET they are often written on top of EF Core.

questions.question: What are IaaS, PaaS and SaaS?
questions.answer:
• IaaS: you rent virtual machines and manage the OS and apps (Azure VMs, AWS EC2).
  • PaaS: you deploy code and the platform manages servers (Azure App Service, Heroku).
  • SaaS: finished software you just use (Gmail, Salesforce).

questions.question: What is serverless?
questions.answer: You write functions and the cloud runs them on demand, scaling automatically. You pay only when they run and don't manage servers. Examples: Azure Functions, AWS Lambda. It's good for event-driven tasks, but cold starts and time limits can be drawbacks.

questions.question: What are environment variables, and why use them?
questions.answer: Configuration values set outside the code, like database URLs, API keys or feature flags. The same code can then run in dev, staging and production with different settings, and secrets stay out of the codebase. In the cloud, secrets usually live in a vault such as Azure Key Vault.

questions.question: What are some core Azure services?
questions.answer:
• App Service: host web apps and APIs.
  • AKS: managed Kubernetes.
  • Azure SQL / Database for PostgreSQL: managed databases.
  • Blob Storage: files and documents.
  • Functions: serverless.
  • Key Vault: secrets.
  • Entra ID: identity and sign-in.
  • Azure DevOps (or GitHub Actions): CI/CD.

questions.question: What does a typical Git branching workflow look like?
questions.answer:
1. Pull the latest main.
  2. Create a feature branch: git checkout -b feature/quote-form.
  3. Commit small changes with clear messages.
  4. Push and open a pull request.
  5. CI runs tests, and a teammate reviews.
  6. Merge into main and delete the branch.

questions.question: What is a pull request, and what makes a good one?
questions.answer: A request to merge your branch, where teammates review the code and CI runs checks before it goes in. A good PR is small and focused, has a clear description of what changed and why, includes tests, and links the ticket.

questions.question: How do you resolve a merge conflict?
questions.answer: Git marks the conflicting lines with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>. Read both versions, keep the right combination (ask the other developer if unsure), remove the markers, run the tests, then git add and commit. Pulling often keeps conflicts small.

questions.question: What do git fetch, pull, stash and reset do?
questions.answer:
• fetch: downloads remote changes without merging.
  • pull: fetch plus merge (or rebase).
  • stash: temporarily saves uncommitted changes.
  • reset: moves your branch back to an earlier commit. --hard discards changes, so be careful.
  • revert: creates a new commit that undoes an old one, which is safe on shared branches.

questions.question: How do you investigate a production bug?
questions.answer: Reproduce it first, with exact steps, environment and data, and check the logs. Narrow it down: front end, API or database? Did it start after a recent release? Fix the root cause, add a test that would have caught it, and check nothing nearby broke. If users are affected, tell the team and stakeholders early.

questions.question: How would you work on a 10-year-old legacy system?
questions.answer: Understand the existing behaviour before changing anything: trace the flow, read logs, use the debugger, and add tests around the area I'm touching. Ask the team about business rules, since the "why" often isn't documented. Make small, careful changes. I'd use AI tools to speed up reading code or writing tests, but not rely on them to fix things.

questions.question: What do you say when you don't know the answer?
questions.answer: "I haven't worked with that directly, but my understanding is…" or "I'd approach it by…". It shows how you think and that you're honest, which matters more than a perfect answer in a junior role.

questions.question: What is semantic HTML, and why does it matter?
questions.answer:
Using elements that describe their meaning, not just their look: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <footer>, <button> instead of a clickable <div>.

  • Accessibility: screen readers use these elements to announce and jump between regions.
  • SEO: search engines understand the page structure.
  • Free behaviour: a real <button> is focusable and works with Enter and Space.
  • Readability: the markup explains itself to the next developer.

questions.question: What's the difference between block and inline elements?
questions.answer:
• Block (<div>, <p>, <h1>, <section>): starts on a new line and takes the full width available. Width, height and vertical margins apply.
  • Inline (<span>, <a>, <strong>): flows inside text and is only as wide as its content. Width and height are ignored.
  • Inline-block: flows like inline but accepts width and height.

CSS display can change any element's behaviour.

questions.question: What does <!DOCTYPE html> do?
questions.answer: It tells the browser to render the page in standards mode using modern HTML rules. Without it, browsers fall back to quirks mode, which imitates old browser bugs, so layout (especially the box model) can behave differently. It must be the first line of the document.

questions.question: What does the viewport meta tag do?
questions.answer:
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

It tells mobile browsers to make the page as wide as the device screen instead of pretending to be a ~980px desktop screen and zooming out. Without it, media queries for small screens don't work as expected.

questions.question: What are data-* attributes?
questions.answer:
Custom attributes for storing extra information on an element, without inventing invalid attributes.

<button data-user-id="42">Delete</button>

btn.dataset.userId // "42"

Values are always strings. Use them for small bits of data your JavaScript or CSS needs, not for large state.

questions.question: What's the difference between async and defer on a script tag?
questions.answer:
Both download the script without blocking HTML parsing. The difference is when it runs:

  • defer: runs after the HTML is fully parsed, in the order the scripts appear, before DOMContentLoaded. Good for app code that needs the DOM.
  • async: runs as soon as it finishes downloading, in any order. Good for independent scripts such as analytics.
  • Neither: parsing stops while the script downloads and runs.

type="module" scripts are deferred by default.

questions.question: How do you make a web page accessible?
questions.answer:
• Use semantic elements and a logical heading order (h1 → h2 …).
  • Give images meaningful alt text (empty alt="" for decorative ones).
  • Label every form field with <label>.
  • Make everything work with the keyboard, with a visible focus outline.
  • Keep enough colour contrast, and don't rely on colour alone.
  • Use ARIA only when no native element fits ("no ARIA is better than bad ARIA").
  • Test with a screen reader and a tool such as Lighthouse or axe.

questions.question: What's the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage and cookies?
questions.answer:
• localStorage: about 5 MB per origin, strings only, stays until cleared. Never sent to the server.
  • sessionStorage: same API, but cleared when the tab closes, and separate per tab.
  • Cookies: small (~4 KB), sent to the server with every matching request, can expire. Can be HttpOnly (hidden from JavaScript), Secure and SameSite.

Don't store auth tokens in localStorage if you can avoid it, because any XSS can read them. An HttpOnly cookie is safer.

questions.question: How do you make a web page load faster?
questions.answer:
• Send less: minify and compress (gzip/Brotli), split code, remove unused JavaScript.
  • Optimise images: modern formats (WebP/AVIF), correct sizes, loading="lazy" below the fold.
  • Cache: long cache headers for hashed files, and a CDN.
  • Don't block rendering: defer scripts, inline critical CSS.
  • Measure with Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals: LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness) and CLS (layout shift).

questions.question: What is HTTPS, and what does TLS protect?
questions.answer:
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. TLS gives three things:

  • Encryption: nobody on the network can read the traffic.
  • Integrity: nobody can change it in transit without being detected.
  • Authentication: the server's certificate, signed by a trusted certificate authority, proves you're talking to the real site.

During the handshake the client checks the certificate and both sides agree on session keys. It doesn't hide which site you visit, and it doesn't make the site's own code secure.

questions.question: What are the access modifiers in Java?
questions.answer:
• public: visible everywhere.
  • protected: same package, plus subclasses.
  • (no modifier) package-private: same package only.
  • private: same class only.

Start with the most restrictive one that works, usually private fields with public methods.

questions.question: What's the contract between equals() and hashCode()?
questions.answer:
If two objects are equals(), they must return the same hashCode(). The reverse isn't required: different objects may share a hash code.

Hash-based collections (HashMap, HashSet) use the hash code to find the bucket, then equals() inside it. If you override equals() without hashCode(), an object you put in a HashSet may never be found again. Records generate both for you.

questions.question: What's the difference between HashMap, Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap?
questions.answer:
• HashMap: not thread-safe, allows one null key and null values. The default choice.
  • Hashtable: legacy. Every method is synchronized, so it's slow under contention. No nulls.
  • ConcurrentHashMap: thread-safe with fine-grained locking, so many threads can read and write at once. No nulls. Has atomic helpers such as computeIfAbsent and merge.

questions.question: What is Optional, and when should you use it?
questions.answer:
A container that may or may not hold a value, used as a return type to make "might be missing" explicit instead of returning null.

Optional<User> u = repo.findById(id);
String name = u.map(User::getName).orElse("Unknown");

Don't use it for fields or method parameters, and avoid calling get() without checking. Prefer orElse, orElseThrow, map and ifPresent.

questions.question: How do you make a class immutable in Java?
questions.answer:
• Make the class final so it can't be subclassed.
  • Make all fields private final, set once in the constructor.
  • No setters.
  • Copy mutable inputs and outputs (e.g. return List.copyOf(items)).

Immutable objects are thread-safe and safe to share or use as map keys. String, Integer and records are examples; a record is the shortest way to write one, as long as its components are immutable too.

questions.question: How do you run work on another thread in Java?
questions.answer:
Avoid creating raw Threads by hand. Use an ExecutorService, which manages a pool of threads:

try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { // closeable since Java 19
  Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> compute());
  int result = f.get();
}

CompletableFuture lets you chain async steps (thenApply, thenCombine). A thread is a path of execution inside a process; threads share the process's memory, which is why shared state needs care.

questions.question: What do synchronized and volatile do?
questions.answer:
• synchronized: only one thread at a time can run the block for a given lock object, and changes made inside are visible to the next thread that takes the lock. Gives mutual exclusion and visibility.
  • volatile: every read sees the latest write to that field, but there's no locking. Good for a simple flag such as volatile boolean running, not for count++, which is read-modify-write.

For counters use AtomicInteger; for more complex cases, ReentrantLock or concurrent collections.

questions.question: What are virtual threads?
questions.answer:
Lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than the operating system, final since Java 21. You can run millions of them. When one blocks on I/O, the JVM parks it and frees the underlying OS thread for another.

try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
  ex.submit(() -> callSlowApi());
}

They suit I/O-heavy servers (one thread per request, simple blocking code) and don't make CPU-heavy work faster. Don't pool them. Since Java 24, blocking inside a synchronized block no longer pins the OS thread, which removed the main early pitfall.

questions.question: What are sealed classes and pattern matching for switch?
questions.answer:
A sealed type (Java 17) lists exactly which classes may extend it. Pattern matching for switch (Java 21) can then check every case, and the compiler complains if one is missing.

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}
record Square(double side) implements Shape {}

double area(Shape s) {
  return switch (s) {
    case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
    case Square q -> q.side() * q.side();
  };
}

questions.question: What's the difference between null and undefined?
questions.answer:
undefined means a value was never assigned: a declared variable, a missing property, a function with no return. null is an intentional "no value" that you set yourself.

null == undefined is true, null === undefined is false. A quirk: typeof null is "object".

questions.question: How do arrow functions differ from regular functions?
questions.answer:
• No own this: they use the this of the surrounding code, which is why they're handy for callbacks.
  • No arguments object (use ...args).
  • Can't be used as constructors with new.
  • Shorter syntax, with an implicit return for one expression: x => x * 2.

Don't use an arrow function as an object method that needs this.

questions.question: What do optional chaining (?.) and nullish coalescing (??) do?
questions.answer:
• a?.b returns undefined instead of throwing if a is null or undefined. Works for calls too: fn?.().
  • a ?? b returns b only when a is null or undefined.

The difference from ||: 0 || 10 is 10, but 0 ?? 10 is 0, so ?? keeps valid falsy values like 0 and "".

questions.question: What is prototypal inheritance?
questions.answer:
Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype. When you read a property the object doesn't have, JavaScript looks up the prototype chain until it finds it or reaches null.

const animal = { speak() { return "..." } };
const dog = Object.create(animal);
dog.speak(); // found on animal

class syntax is built on top of this: methods live on ClassName.prototype, shared by all instances.

questions.question: What's the difference between microtasks and macrotasks?
questions.answer:
After each task, the event loop empties the whole microtask queue before running the next macrotask.

  • Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events.
  • Microtasks: promise callbacks (.then, code after await), queueMicrotask.
setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout"));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("promise"));
console.log("sync");
// sync, promise, timeout

questions.question: What are debounce and throttle?
questions.answer:
• Debounce: wait until the calls stop for a set time, then run once. Example: search as you type, firing 300 ms after the last keystroke.
  • Throttle: run at most once per set time while calls keep coming. Example: handling scroll or resize every 100 ms.

Both limit how often an expensive function runs when an event fires many times a second.

questions.question: What is event delegation?
questions.answer:
Instead of adding a listener to every child, add one to a parent and check event.target. It works because most events bubble up from the element that was clicked through its ancestors.

list.addEventListener("click", e => {
  const item = e.target.closest("li");
  if (item) select(item.dataset.id);
});

Fewer listeners, and items added later work automatically.

questions.question: What do Promise.all, allSettled, race and any do?
questions.answer:
• all: waits for every promise; rejects as soon as one fails.
  • allSettled: waits for every promise and gives each one's result or error. Never rejects.
  • race: settles with whichever promise settles first, success or failure. Handy for timeouts.
  • any: resolves with the first success; rejects only if all fail.

Use them to run independent async work in parallel instead of awaiting one at a time.

questions.question: What's the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
questions.answer:
A shallow copy copies the top level only, so nested objects are still shared: {...obj}, [...arr], Object.assign.

A deep copy copies everything, so changing a nested value doesn't affect the original. Use structuredClone(obj): it handles dates, Maps, Sets and circular references, but throws on functions and DOM nodes, and class instances come back as plain objects. JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) also works for plain data but loses dates, undefined, functions, Maps and Sets.

questions.question: What are generics in TypeScript?
questions.answer:
Type parameters that let one function or type work with many types while keeping type safety.

function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}
const n = first([1, 2, 3]); // n is number | undefined

You can constrain them with <T extends { id: string }>. Without generics you'd have to use any and lose the type.

questions.question: What is Node.js?
questions.answer:
A JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine that runs JavaScript outside the browser. It uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model, so one process can handle many connections at once.

Used for APIs, real-time apps (chat, websockets), command-line tools and build tooling. It's not a framework; Express, Fastify and NestJS are frameworks built on it.

questions.question: How does Node.js handle many requests on a single thread?
questions.answer:
Your JavaScript runs on one thread, but slow work such as network and file I/O is handed off: the operating system or libuv's thread pool does the waiting. When the result is ready, a callback is queued and the event loop runs it.

So the thread is never sitting idle waiting for a database. The catch: CPU-heavy code (big loops, image processing, sync crypto) blocks the one thread, and every request waits.

questions.question: What are the phases of the Node.js event loop?
questions.answer:
1. Timers: setTimeout and setInterval callbacks that are due.
  2. Pending callbacks: some deferred system callbacks.
  3. Poll: waits for and runs I/O callbacks.
  4. Check: setImmediate callbacks.
  5. Close callbacks: e.g. socket.on("close").

Between each callback, Node empties the process.nextTick queue and then the promise microtask queue.

questions.question: What's the difference between process.nextTick, setImmediate and setTimeout(fn, 0)?
questions.answer:
• process.nextTick: runs right after the current operation, before promise callbacks and before the event loop continues. Overusing it can starve I/O.
  • setImmediate: runs in the check phase, after I/O polling.
  • setTimeout(fn, 0): runs in the timers phase, after at least 1 ms.

From the main module, the order of setImmediate and setTimeout(0) isn't guaranteed. Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs first.

questions.question: What are package.json and package-lock.json?
questions.answer:
• package.json: the project's name, scripts (npm run dev) and dependencies with allowed version ranges.
  • package-lock.json: the exact version of every installed package, including dependencies of dependencies, so every machine installs the same tree.

Commit both. Use npm ci in CI: it installs exactly what the lock file says. dependencies are needed at runtime; devDependencies only for building and testing.

questions.question: What do ^ and ~ mean in package.json versions?
questions.answer:
Versions follow semver: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (breaking.feature.fix).

  • ^1.4.2: any 1.x.x from 1.4.2 up; minor and patch updates are allowed. The npm default.
  • ~1.4.2: any 1.4.x from 1.4.2 up; patch updates only.
  • 1.4.2: exactly that version.

Before 1.0, ^ is stricter: ^0.4.2 allows only 0.4.x, because a 0.x minor release may break things.

questions.question: What's the difference between CommonJS and ES modules in Node?
questions.answer:
• CommonJS: require() and module.exports. Loads synchronously. Node's original system.
  • ES modules: import and export. The JavaScript standard, also used in browsers. Supports top-level await, and imports can be analysed statically (tree shaking).

Node treats a file as an ES module if it ends in .mjs, or if package.json has "type": "module". ES modules can import CommonJS, and since Node 22 CommonJS can require() an ES module too, as long as it has no top-level await. New projects usually choose ES modules.

questions.question: What is Express, and what is middleware?
questions.answer:
Express is a minimal web framework for Node. Middleware is a function that runs on the way to your route handler: it can read or change the request, end the response, or call next() to pass control on.

app.use(express.json());           // parse JSON bodies
app.use((req, res, next) => {      // log every request
  console.log(req.method, req.url);
  next();
});
app.get("/users/:id", getUser);

Middleware runs in the order it's registered.

questions.question: How do you handle errors in Express?
questions.answer:
Add an error-handling middleware with four arguments, registered after your routes:

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(err);
  res.status(err.status || 500).json({ error: "Something went wrong" });
});

In Express 4, errors thrown in async handlers must be passed on with next(err) or they become unhandled rejections. Express 5 forwards rejected promises to the error handler automatically. Don't send stack traces to clients in production.

questions.question: What are streams in Node.js?
questions.answer:
A way to process data piece by piece instead of loading it all into memory. Four kinds: Readable (file read, HTTP request), Writable (file write, HTTP response), Duplex (socket) and Transform (gzip).

import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";
await pipeline(
  fs.createReadStream("big.log"),
  zlib.createGzip(),
  fs.createWriteStream("big.log.gz")
);

pipeline handles backpressure and cleans up all the streams if one fails.

questions.question: What is a Buffer in Node.js?
questions.answer:
A fixed-size chunk of raw binary data, used for files, network packets and images. Strings are text; Buffers are bytes.

const b = Buffer.from("hi", "utf8"); // <Buffer 68 69>
b.toString("base64");               // "aGk="

Most file and network APIs give you Buffers unless you ask for an encoding.

questions.question: What is EventEmitter?
questions.answer:
Node's built-in implementation of the observer pattern. An object emits named events and listeners react to them. Streams, HTTP servers and sockets are all EventEmitters.

import { EventEmitter } from "node:events";
const orders = new EventEmitter();
orders.on("created", o => sendEmail(o));
orders.emit("created", { id: 1 });

Listeners run synchronously in the order they were added. An "error" event with no listener crashes the process.

questions.question: How do you run CPU-heavy work in Node without blocking the event loop?
questions.answer:
• worker_threads: run JavaScript on separate threads inside the same process; pass data with messages. Best for CPU work such as image resizing or parsing.
  • child_process: run a separate program or script.
  • cluster (or a process manager such as PM2): run one Node process per CPU core behind one port, to use all cores for handling requests.
  • Move it to a job queue (e.g. BullMQ with Redis) processed by a separate worker.

Async functions don't help here: async code still runs on the main thread.

questions.question: How do you manage configuration and secrets in a Node app?
questions.answer:
Read them from environment variables (process.env.DATABASE_URL), never hard-code them. Locally, keep them in a .env file listed in .gitignore. Load it with node --env-file=.env app.js (built in since Node 20.6) or the dotenv package.

Validate the required values at startup so the app fails fast. In production, use the platform's secret store.

questions.question: How do you handle async errors and unhandled rejections in Node?
questions.answer:
• Wrap await in try/catch, or add .catch() to promises you don't await.
  • Since Node 15, an unhandled promise rejection crashes the process by default.
  • Use process.on("unhandledRejection") and process.on("uncaughtException") to log the error, then exit and let a process manager restart the app. The state after an uncaught exception can't be trusted.

questions.question: How do you secure a Node.js API?
questions.answer:
• Validate all input (e.g. with Zod or Joi).
  • Use parameterised queries or an ORM to prevent SQL injection.
  • Set security headers with helmet, and configure CORS narrowly.
  • Rate-limit login and other sensitive routes.
  • Hash passwords with bcrypt or argon2.
  • Keep secrets in environment variables; run npm audit and update dependencies.
  • Don't leak stack traces; run with NODE_ENV=production.

questions.question: How does JWT authentication work in a Node API?
questions.answer:
1. The user logs in; the server checks the password and signs a token: jwt.sign({ sub: user.id }, secret, { expiresIn: "15m" }).
  2. The client sends it on each request: Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  3. Middleware verifies the signature and expiry with jwt.verify and sets req.user.

A JWT is signed, not encrypted, so anyone can read its contents: don't put secrets in it. Keep access tokens short-lived and use a refresh token to get new ones.

questions.question: How do you test a Node.js app?
questions.answer:
• Test runner: the built-in node:test (stable since Node 20), Jest or Vitest.
  • Unit tests for pure functions; mock external services.
  • API tests with supertest, which calls your Express app without starting a real server.
  • Integration tests against a real test database (e.g. in Docker).
  • Run them in CI on every pull request.

questions.question: How would you find a memory leak in a Node.js app?
questions.answer:
1. Confirm it: memory (process.memoryUsage().heapUsed) keeps growing under steady load.
  2. Take heap snapshots a few minutes apart (Chrome DevTools via node --inspect) and compare them to see which objects keep growing.
  3. Common causes: caches or arrays that never shrink, event listeners added and never removed, timers that are never cleared, and closures holding large objects.

Fix the cause; don't just raise --max-old-space-size.

questions.question: Why prefer fs/promises over fs.readFileSync in a server?
questions.answer:
readFileSync blocks the event loop until the file is read, so every other request waits. fs/promises does the work in the background:

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
const text = await readFile("data.json", "utf8");

Sync versions are fine in startup code and command-line scripts, where nothing else is waiting. For large files, use streams.

questions.question: What's the difference between const and readonly in C#?
questions.answer:
• const: set at compile time and implicitly static. Only for built-in types such as numbers, bool, char and string, and enums. The value is copied into every assembly that uses it, so changing it means recompiling those too.
  • readonly: set at declaration or in the constructor, can be any type, and can differ per instance.

Use const for values that truly never change (MaxRetries = 3), and readonly for everything else.

questions.question: What are extension methods in C#?
questions.answer:
Static methods that look like instance methods on a type you don't own. The first parameter has this.

public static class StringExtensions {
  public static bool IsBlank(this string? s) => string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s);
}
"  ".IsBlank(); // true

LINQ is built entirely from extension methods on IEnumerable<T>.

questions.question: What's the difference between an abstract class and an interface in C#?
questions.answer:
• Abstract class: can have fields, constructors and implemented methods. A class can inherit only one.
  • Interface: a contract. A class can implement many. Since C# 8 it can include default method implementations, but still no instance fields.

Use an interface to define a capability (IPaymentService), which also makes dependency injection and mocking easy. Use an abstract class to share code between closely related types.

questions.question: What are boxing and unboxing?
questions.answer:
Boxing wraps a value type (such as int) in an object on the heap so it can be treated as object. Unboxing extracts it again.

int n = 5;
object o = n;     // boxing
int m = (int)o;   // unboxing

Each box is a heap allocation, so it costs memory and time in hot loops. Generics (List<int> instead of ArrayList) avoid it.

questions.question: What are the Transient, Scoped and Singleton lifetimes in ASP.NET Core?
questions.answer:
• Transient: a new instance every time it's requested.
  • Scoped: one instance per HTTP request. DbContext is registered this way.
  • Singleton: one instance for the whole app. Must be thread-safe.

Never inject a scoped service into a singleton (a "captive dependency"): the scoped object would live forever and be shared between requests.

questions.question: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core, and why does order matter?
questions.answer:
Middleware components form a pipeline. Each one can handle the request, pass it to the next with await next(), and act on the response on the way back.

They run in the order registered in Program.cs, so order matters: exception handling goes first to catch everything, and UseAuthentication() must come before UseAuthorization(), both before the endpoints they protect. A typical order: exception handler → HTTPS redirection → static files → routing → CORS → authentication → authorization → endpoints.

questions.question: What's the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable?
questions.answer:
• IEnumerable<T>: runs in memory. LINQ operators are C# code executed on objects already loaded.
  • IQueryable<T>: builds an expression tree that a provider (e.g. EF Core) translates, usually into SQL, and runs in the database.

Calling .ToList() or .AsEnumerable() too early on an EF query loads every row and then filters in memory. Keep filtering (Where, Take) on the IQueryable.

questions.question: What are records in C#?
questions.answer:
Types designed for data, added in C# 9. They have value equality (two records with the same values are equal), a readable ToString(), and non-destructive copies with with.

public record Quote(string Id, decimal Premium);
var q2 = q1 with { Premium = 120m };

Good for DTOs and immutable values. record struct (C# 10) is the value-type version.

questions.question: What are nullable reference types in C#?
questions.answer:
A compiler feature (C# 8, on by default in new projects) that makes null intent explicit: string should never be null, string? might be. The compiler warns when you might dereference null or assign null to a non-nullable type.

It doesn't change runtime behaviour; it's static analysis. Use ?., ?? and null checks to handle the nullable cases.

questions.question: What is IDisposable, and what does a using statement do?
questions.answer:
IDisposable is for objects that hold unmanaged resources such as files, database connections and sockets, which the garbage collector won't release promptly. using calls Dispose() automatically, even if an exception is thrown.

using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs);
await conn.OpenAsync();
// disposed at the end of the scope

Exception: don't wrap HttpClient in using per request. Use IHttpClientFactory.

questions.question: What are delegates, Func, Action and events?
questions.answer:
• A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method.
  • Func<T, TResult>: built-in delegate that returns a value. Action<T>: returns nothing. Lambdas are usually passed as these, e.g. in LINQ.
  • An event is a delegate that outside code can only subscribe to (+=) or unsubscribe from (-=), not invoke.
Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;
button.Click += (s, e) => Save();

questions.question: What are minimal APIs in ASP.NET Core?
questions.answer:
A lightweight way to build HTTP APIs without controllers, added in .NET 6. Routes map straight to lambdas in Program.cs, with dependency injection and model binding in the parameters.

app.MapGet("/quotes/{id}", async (string id, IQuoteService svc) =>
  await svc.Find(id) is { } q ? Results.Ok(q) : Results.NotFound());

Good for small services and microservices. Controllers still suit large APIs with many filters and conventions.

questions.question: How do EF Core migrations work?
questions.answer:
Migrations turn changes to your C# model into versioned database schema changes.

  1. Change the entity classes.
  2. dotnet ef migrations add AddPolicyStatus generates a migration with Up and Down methods.
  3. Review it, then apply it with dotnet ef database update, or generate a SQL script for production.

Commit migrations to source control. EF stores which ones were applied in the __EFMigrationsHistory table.

questions.question: What are common async/await mistakes in C#?
questions.answer:
• .Result or .Wait() on a task: blocks a thread and can deadlock where there's a synchronization context. Use await all the way up.
  • async void: exceptions can't be caught by the caller. Use it only for event handlers; return Task otherwise.
  • Task.Run in ASP.NET Core to "make it async": just moves work to another thread-pool thread. Await real async I/O instead.
  • Forgetting to pass a CancellationToken to long operations.
  • Awaiting independent calls one by one instead of using Task.WhenAll.

questions.question: How does garbage collection work in .NET?
questions.answer:
The GC frees objects that are no longer reachable. The managed heap is split into generations:

  • Gen 0: new objects. Collected often and fast; most objects die here.
  • Gen 1: a buffer between short- and long-lived objects.
  • Gen 2: long-lived objects. Collected rarely and more expensively.
  • Large Object Heap: objects of 85,000 bytes or more, collected with Gen 2.

The GC doesn't close files or connections; that's what IDisposable is for.

questions.question: How does configuration work in ASP.NET Core?
questions.answer:
Values are merged from several sources, later ones winning: appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (in development), environment variables, then command-line arguments.

Bind a section to a class with the options pattern:

builder.Services.Configure<SmtpOptions>(
  builder.Configuration.GetSection("Smtp"));
// inject IOptions<SmtpOptions> where needed

Keep secrets out of appsettings.json; use user secrets locally and a vault such as Azure Key Vault in production.

questions.question: How do you copy or update objects and arrays in JavaScript without changing the original?
questions.answer:
Objects and arrays are reference values: assigning one to a new variable copies the reference, not the data, so both variables point at the same object and a change through one shows up in the other. (Strictly, JavaScript passes everything by value; for an object, that value is the reference.)

To change something without affecting the original, copy it first:

  • Shallow copy for flat data: { ...obj }, [...arr] or Object.assign({}, obj). Nested objects are still shared.
  • Deep copy for nested data: structuredClone(obj). It can't copy functions or DOM nodes, and class instances come back as plain objects.
  • Arrays: use non-mutating methods such as map, filter, slice, concat and the ES2023 toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with, instead of sort, reverse, splice or push, which change the array in place.
const next = { ...user, address: { ...user.address, city: "Sydney" } };
const sorted = scores.toSorted((a, b) => a - b); // scores is unchanged
setItems([...items, newItem]);                    // React: a new array

This matters most in React: it decides whether to re-render by comparing references, so mutating state in place can leave the UI stale. Vue 3 tracks changes made in place on reactive state, so mutation does re-render there, but you must never mutate props, and immutable updates still make changes easier to follow.

questions.question: What are the rules of hooks?
questions.answer:
• Only call hooks at the top level of a component or custom hook: never inside conditions, loops or nested functions.
  • Only call them from React function components or other custom hooks.

React identifies each hook by the order it's called, so the order must be the same on every render. A custom hook is just a function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks, e.g. useFetch(url). The ESLint plugin eslint-plugin-react-hooks catches mistakes.

questions.question: What's the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components?
questions.answer:
• Controlled: React state holds the input's value, and every change goes through a handler. Easy to validate or format as the user types.
  • Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value, and you read it when needed (with a ref or FormData on submit). Less code for simple forms.
const [email, setEmail] = useState("");
<input value={email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)} />

Form libraries such as React Hook Form mostly use uncontrolled inputs for performance.

questions.question: What do useMemo, useCallback and React.memo do?
questions.answer:
• useMemo: caches a computed value between renders until its dependencies change.
  • useCallback: caches a function, so a child receives the same function each render.
  • React.memo: skips re-rendering a component when its props haven't changed (compared by reference).

They work together: React.memo only helps if the props you pass are stable, which is what useCallback/useMemo provide. Use them when you've measured a slow render, not everywhere. The React Compiler (React 19 era) can add this memoisation automatically.

questions.question: What is prop drilling, and how does Context help?
questions.answer:
Prop drilling is passing a value down through several components that don't use it, just to reach one deep inside. Context lets a parent provide a value that any descendant can read directly with useContext.

const ThemeContext = createContext("light");
<ThemeContext value="dark"><App /></ThemeContext>   // React 19; earlier: ThemeContext.Provider
const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);

Good for app-wide values like the theme, the signed-in user or the language. Every consumer re-renders when the value changes, so for large, frequently changing state teams often use a store such as Zustand or Redux Toolkit.

questions.question: What is useRef used for?
questions.answer:
useRef gives you a box (ref.current) that keeps its value between renders, and changing it does not trigger a re-render. Two common uses:

  • Getting a DOM element: <input ref={inputRef} />, then inputRef.current.focus().
  • Storing a mutable value that isn't shown on screen, such as a timer ID or the previous value of a prop.

If changing it should update the UI, it belongs in state instead.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer:
A 60–90 second story that ends with why you're in this interview, not your life history. A simple shape:

  • Present: who you are now ("I'm a graduate developer who's just finished a software engineering degree").
  • Past: one or two things that prove it, ideally a project with a result ("I built a booking app used by a local gym").
  • Future: why this role ("I want to work on a product team using React and .NET, which is what you do").

Practise it out loud until it sounds natural, and tailor the last part to each company.

questions.question: Tell me about a challenging project you worked on.
questions.answer:
Use STAR and keep the focus on what you did:

  • Situation: the project and why it mattered (one or two sentences).
