  • Task: the hard part you were responsible for.
  • Action: the specific steps you took, the decisions and why, including anything technical.
  • Result: the outcome, with a number if you can ("load time went from 6 s to 1.5 s"), and what you learned.

Pick a story where something went wrong and you fixed it; it's more convincing than one where everything went smoothly. Keep it to about two minutes.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you made a mistake.
questions.answer:
Interviewers want to see ownership and learning, not perfection. Pick a real but recoverable mistake (not a disaster, and not a disguised strength like "I work too hard").

  • Say plainly what happened and that it was your mistake.
  • Explain how you noticed it and what you did straight away to fix it.
  • Finish with what you changed afterwards: a test, a checklist, asking for review earlier.

Example: "I deployed a change without running the migrations, the app errored for ten minutes, I rolled back, fixed it, and added the migration step to our deploy script."

questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate.
questions.answer:
Show that you can disagree respectfully and put the outcome ahead of being right.

  • Situation: what you disagreed about (keep it technical or practical, not personal).
  • Action: you listened to their reasons, explained yours with evidence (a quick prototype, data, the docs), and looked for common ground, or escalated calmly if needed.
  • Result: what was decided and how it turned out, even if it was their idea.

Never criticise the other person. "We went with their approach and it was the right call" is a perfectly good ending.

questions.question: How do you learn a new technology quickly?
questions.answer:
Give a real example, then your method:

  • Start with the official docs or tutorial to learn the core ideas, not every detail.
  • Build something small straight away, because you learn by hitting problems.
  • Read existing code in the team's project to see how it's used in practice.
  • Ask teammates when stuck after a reasonable try, and write down what you learned.

Example: "For my last project I had to learn Docker in a week. I did the official getting-started guide, containerised our API, then got a teammate to review the Dockerfile."

questions.question: What are the values of the CSS position property?
questions.answer:
• static: the default; normal document flow.
  • relative: stays in the flow, but can be nudged with top/left; also becomes the reference point for absolutely positioned children.
  • absolute: taken out of the flow and placed relative to the nearest positioned ancestor.
  • fixed: placed relative to the viewport; stays put when you scroll.
  • sticky: behaves like relative until you scroll past a threshold, then sticks (e.g. table headers).

questions.question: How do you centre an element horizontally and vertically?
questions.answer:
With Flexbox or Grid on the parent:

.parent { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; }
/* or */
.parent { display: grid; place-items: center; }

For horizontal centring of a block with a fixed width, margin: 0 auto also works. The parent needs a height for vertical centring to be visible.

questions.question: What's the difference between px, em and rem?
questions.answer:
• px: a fixed size.
  • em: relative to the font size of the element's parent (for font-size) or the element itself (for other properties), so nested em values compound.
  • rem: relative to the root (html) font size, usually 16px, so 1.5rem is 24px everywhere.

Use rem for font sizes and spacing so the page scales when the user increases their browser's font size; em for things that should scale with their own text, like padding on a button.

questions.question: What's the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
questions.answer:
• DELETE: removes rows, optionally with a WHERE. Logged row by row, fires triggers, and can be rolled back in a transaction.
  • TRUNCATE: removes all rows at once. Much faster, usually resets identity counters, and doesn't fire row triggers.
  • DROP: removes the whole table, including its structure and indexes.

Always check the WHERE clause before running a DELETE on real data: run it as a SELECT first.

questions.question: How would you find duplicate rows in a table?
questions.answer:
Group by the columns that should be unique and keep the groups with more than one row:

SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM customers
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

To see every duplicate row with its id, use a window function: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) and keep rows where the number is greater than 1. Then add a UNIQUE constraint so it can't happen again.

questions.question: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?
questions.answer:
Inheritance is an "is-a" relationship: a subclass gets everything from its parent. Composition is a "has-a" relationship: a class holds other objects and delegates work to them.

  • Inheritance couples classes tightly: a change in the parent can break every subclass, and deep hierarchies get hard to follow.
  • Composition is flexible: you can swap parts (inject a different PaymentGateway) and test them separately.

Use inheritance for a true "is-a" with shared behaviour; reach for composition and interfaces by default.

questions.question: What are React Server Components, and how are they different from server-side rendering?
questions.answer:
Server Components run only on the server (at build time or per request). Their code is never sent to the browser, they can be async and read data directly (a database, the file system), but they can't use state, effects or event handlers. Components that need interactivity are marked "use client".

SSR is different: it renders client components to HTML on the server for a fast first load, then ships their JavaScript and hydrates them in the browser. Server Components are never hydrated, so they add nothing to the bundle. Frameworks such as Next.js (App Router) use both together.

questions.question: What are Actions in React 19, and what do useActionState and useOptimistic do?
questions.answer:
An Action is an async function you hand to React, for example as a form's action. React tracks its pending state and errors and resets the form when it succeeds, which replaces a lot of hand-written loading and error state.

  • useActionState(action, initialState) returns [state, formAction, isPending]: the last result (such as a validation message), the action to pass to the form, and whether it's running.
  • useOptimistic shows the expected result straight away (a liked post, a sent message) and rolls back automatically if the action fails.
const [error, submit, isPending] = useActionState(saveProfile, null);
<form action={submit}>…<button disabled={isPending}>Save</button></form>

questions.question: What does the use() API do in React 19?
questions.answer:
use reads the value of a promise or a context during render. With a promise, the component suspends until it resolves, and the nearest <Suspense> shows its fallback meanwhile; a rejection goes to the nearest error boundary.

function Comments({ commentsPromise }) {
  const comments = use(commentsPromise);
  return comments.map(c => <p key={c.id}>{c.text}</p>);
}

Unlike hooks, use can be called inside conditions and loops. Don't create the promise during render (it would be new every time): it should come from a parent, a framework or a cache.

questions.question: What do useTransition and useDeferredValue do?
questions.answer:
They tell React that some updates are less urgent, so typing and clicking stay responsive while slower rendering happens in the background (concurrent rendering).

  • useTransition gives you startTransition to wrap a state update you control, plus isPending to show a spinner: startTransition(() => setTab("reports")).
  • useDeferredValue gives you a lagging copy of a value you receive, e.g. filter a big list with useDeferredValue(query) while the input itself updates instantly.

Urgent updates (the text in an input) interrupt a transition that's still rendering.

questions.question: What is Suspense in React?
questions.answer:
<Suspense fallback={…}> shows a fallback (a spinner, a skeleton) while something inside it isn't ready yet, then swaps in the real content.

  • Code splitting: const Chart = lazy(() => import("./Chart")) loads a component only when it's first shown.
  • Data: components that read a promise with use, or framework data loading, suspend until the data arrives.
  • Streaming: with server rendering, each Suspense boundary can be sent to the browser as soon as it's ready.

Place boundaries where a loading state makes sense to the user, not around every component.

questions.question: What's new in the recent Java LTS releases (17, 21 and 25)?
questions.answer:
• Java 17: records, sealed classes, text blocks ("""), pattern matching for instanceof, switch expressions. Still a common enterprise baseline.
  • Java 21: virtual threads, pattern matching for switch, record patterns, sequenced collections (getFirst(), reversed()).
  • Java 25 (the latest LTS, September 2025): compact source files and instance main methods (a program can be just void main() { … }), flexible constructor bodies (statements before super(…)), module import declarations and scoped values.

Good to say which version your last project used and one feature you actually relied on.

questions.question: What's new in recent C# versions (12, 13 and 14)?
questions.answer:
• C# 12 (.NET 8): primary constructors for classes (class OrderService(IRepo repo)) and collection expressions (int[] xs = [1, 2, 3];).
  • C# 13 (.NET 9): params works with any collection type, and a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type.
  • C# 14 (.NET 10): extension members (extension properties, not just methods), the field keyword for a property's backing field, and null-conditional assignment (customer?.Order = order;).

Be ready to say which version your project used; interviewers mostly want to see that you keep up, not a full list.

questions.question: An ASP.NET Core API gets slow under load, but CPU is low. What could be happening?
questions.answer:
A classic cause is thread pool starvation. Each request runs on a thread-pool thread; if code blocks on async work (.Result, .Wait(), synchronous database or HTTP calls), threads sit idle waiting. New requests queue for a free thread, so latency climbs while the CPU does almost nothing. The pool adds threads only slowly.

  • Confirm it: dotnet-counters shows a growing thread-pool queue and thread count.
  • Fix it: async all the way down, no sync-over-async, and async versions of I/O calls.
  • Also check: slow database queries or missing indexes, connection-pool exhaustion, and a dependency that has started timing out.

questions.question: What's the difference between JavaScript in the browser and in Node.js?
questions.answer:
It's the same language (both often run on V8), but the environment differs:

  • Browser: the DOM (document), window, user events, and a sandbox with no file-system access.
  • Node.js: no DOM, but modules for files, networking and processes (fs, http, process), and access to the machine it runs on.

Both have fetch, timers, promises and ES modules, and globalThis refers to the global object in each (window in the browser, global in Node).

questions.question: What is callback hell, and how do you avoid it?
questions.answer:
Deeply nested callbacks, each async step inside the previous one's callback, often with error handling repeated at every level. The code drifts right and gets hard to read and maintain.

// Instead of readFile(a, (err, x) => { parse(x, (err, y) => { save(y, …) }) })
const x = await readFile(a, "utf8");
const y = await parse(x);
await save(y);

Use promises and async/await (with try/catch), the promise versions of Node APIs (fs/promises, or util.promisify for older callback APIs), and small named functions.

questions.question: How would you design a URL shortener?
questions.answer:
Start with the requirements (create a short link, redirect quickly, maybe count clicks), then a simple design:

  • API: POST /links with the long URL returns a short code; GET /{code} answers with a redirect (302, or 301 if links never change).
  • Short code: encode an auto-increment id in base62 (a–z, A–Z, 0–9), or generate a random 7-character code and retry on a collision.
  • Storage: a table of code → long URL, created_at, owner, with the code as the primary key.
  • Speed: redirects are read-heavy, so cache popular codes in Redis.
  • Extras: count clicks asynchronously (a queue), rate-limit creation, and validate URLs to stop abuse.

Talk through trade-offs as you go; there's no single right answer.

questions.question: What is caching, and where can you add it?
questions.answer:
Keeping a copy of data somewhere faster so you don't recompute or refetch it. Common layers:

  • Browser: HTTP cache headers (Cache-Control, ETag).
  • CDN: static files and public pages served from servers near the user.
  • Application: an in-memory or Redis cache for expensive queries, usually cache-aside: check the cache, on a miss read the database and store the result with a TTL.
  • Database: its own buffer cache, plus read replicas.

The hard part is invalidation: decide how stale data may be (the TTL), and clear or update entries when the data changes.

questions.question: What's the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
questions.answer:
• Vertical (scale up): a bigger machine, with more CPU and memory. Simple, but there's a ceiling and it's a single point of failure.
  • Horizontal (scale out): more machines behind a load balancer. Scales further and survives one machine failing.

Horizontal scaling needs stateless app servers: keep sessions in a shared store (Redis) or tokens, not in one server's memory. Databases are harder to scale out; read replicas, caching and, later, partitioning help.

questions.question: An API endpoint has become slow in production. How do you find out why?
questions.answer:
1. Measure first: which endpoint, since when, for everyone or some users? Check monitoring (response times, error rates) and recent deployments.
  2. Find where the time goes: traces or logs with timings show whether it's the database, an external API or the code itself.
  3. Check the usual suspects: a slow query or missing index (look at the query plan), N+1 queries, a dependency timing out, too little memory or too few connections, and blocking calls.
  4. Fix and verify: change one thing, measure again, and add an alert so you hear about it sooner next time.

questions.question: Given an array and a target, how do you find two numbers that add up to the target?
questions.answer:
Brute force checks every pair: O(n²). Better: walk the array once and keep a hash map of numbers seen so far. For each number, check whether target - number is already in the map: O(n) time, O(n) space.

function twoSum(nums, target) {
  const seen = new Map(); // value -> index
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    const need = target - nums[i];
    if (seen.has(need)) return [seen.get(need), i];
    seen.set(nums[i], i);
  }
  return [];
}

The pattern to name: a hash map removes the inner loop. If the array is sorted, two pointers work with O(1) space.

questions.question: How do you check whether the brackets in a string are balanced?
questions.answer:
Use a stack: push each opening bracket; for each closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener. At the end the stack must be empty. O(n) time.

function isBalanced(s) {
  const pairs = { ")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{" };
  const stack = [];
  for (const ch of s) {
    if ("([{".includes(ch)) stack.push(ch);
    else if (ch in pairs && stack.pop() !== pairs[ch]) return false;
  }
  return stack.length === 0;
}

questions.question: What is the sliding window technique?
questions.answer:
Keep a window (a start and an end index) over an array or string, and move it instead of re-checking every subarray. The end moves forward one step at a time; the start moves forward when the window breaks a rule. Usually O(n) instead of O(n²).

Example: the length of the longest substring with no repeated characters.

function longestUnique(s) {
  const last = new Map(); // char -> last index
  let start = 0, best = 0;
  for (let end = 0; end < s.length; end++) {
    if (last.has(s[end]) && last.get(s[end]) >= start) start = last.get(s[end]) + 1;
    last.set(s[end], end);
    best = Math.max(best, end - start + 1);
  }
  return best;
}

questions.question: What is the two-pointer technique?
questions.answer:
Use two indexes that move through the data, often from both ends towards the middle, to avoid a nested loop. Typical uses: checking a palindrome, finding a pair with a given sum in a sorted array, removing duplicates in place, or merging two sorted lists.

function isPalindrome(s) {
  let i = 0, j = s.length - 1;
  while (i < j) {
    if (s[i] !== s[j]) return false;
    i++; j--;
  }
  return true;
}

O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

questions.question: How do you reverse a linked list?
questions.answer:
Walk the list once and turn each next pointer around, keeping track of the previous node. O(n) time, O(1) space.

function reverse(head) {
  let prev = null;
  while (head) {
    const next = head.next; // remember the rest of the list
    head.next = prev;       // point this node backwards
    prev = head;
    head = next;
  }
  return prev; // the new head
}

Draw the three pointers on paper as you explain it; interviewers like seeing that.

questions.question: What's the difference between BFS and DFS?
questions.answer:
• Breadth-first search visits nodes level by level using a queue. It finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph and suits "nearest" or level-order problems.
  • Depth-first search goes as deep as possible before backtracking, using recursion or a stack. It suits exploring every path, detecting cycles, topological sorting and counting connected regions (like islands in a grid).

Both are O(V + E). On a graph, keep a visited set so you don't loop forever.

questions.question: How would you find the k most frequent elements in an array?
questions.answer:
1. Count each value with a hash map: O(n).
  2. Pick the top k counts:
    • Sort the entries by count: O(n log n), simplest.
    • Keep a min-heap of size k: O(n log k), good when k is small.
    • Bucket sort by count (index = frequency): O(n).
const counts = new Map();
for (const x of nums) counts.set(x, (counts.get(x) || 0) + 1);
return [...counts].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, k).map(([x]) => x);

Start with the simple version, then mention the faster ones.

questions.question: How would you implement a circular (ring) buffer?
questions.answer:
A fixed-size array with a head (next item to read), a tail (next free slot) and a size. Both indexes wrap around with % capacity, so adding and removing are O(1) and nothing is ever shifted. Decide what happens when it's full: reject the new item, or overwrite the oldest (common for logs and audio).

class RingBuffer<T> {
  private final Object[] items;
  private int head, tail, size;
  RingBuffer(int capacity) { items = new Object[capacity]; }

  boolean offer(T x) {
    if (size == items.length) return false; // full
    items[tail] = x;
    tail = (tail + 1) % items.length;
    size++;
    return true;
  }

  @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
  T poll() {
    if (size == 0) return null; // empty
    T x = (T) items[head];
    items[head] = null;
    head = (head + 1) % items.length;
    size--;
    return x;
  }
}

questions.question: Why do you want to be a software developer?
questions.answer:
Give a genuine, specific reason and connect it to the job, in under a minute:

  • A moment that got you hooked (automating something tedious, building something people used).
  • What you enjoy about the work now: solving problems, learning constantly, seeing users benefit.
  • How this role fits: the product, the stack, or the kind of team.

Avoid answers only about salary or "I've always loved computers" with nothing concrete behind it.

questions.question: What questions should you ask at the end of an interview?
questions.answer:
Always have two or three ready; "no questions" reads as low interest. Good ones are about the work and how you'd grow:

  • "What would my first few months look like, and what does success look like by then?"
  • "How does the team review code and release changes?"
  • "How do juniors get support: mentoring, pairing, code review?"
  • "What's the biggest challenge the team is working on right now?"

Leave salary and leave entitlements for later rounds unless they bring it up.

questions.question: How do you use AI coding assistants in your work?
questions.answer:
Interviewers want to hear that you use them to go faster without handing over your judgement:

  • Good uses: boilerplate, explaining unfamiliar code or errors, drafting tests, and exploring options.
  • You read and understand every line before it goes in, and you test it; you're responsible for the code, not the tool.
  • You follow the company's policy on what code and data may be shared, and never paste secrets or customer data.
  • You still build the fundamentals yourself, so you can tell when the suggestion is wrong.

A short example of a time it helped, and a time you caught it being wrong, makes the answer convincing.
